planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; the monogerm seed produces a single seedling per node, so stands need little or no thinning even at close spacing.

directions: Kestrel is a widely grown market hybrid beet valued for its true monogerm seed, smooth dark-red globe roots, and dependable resistance to premature bolting when spring temperatures swing warm and cold. Sow thinly 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and keep the bed evenly moist through germination, since the single-seedling habit removes the usual thinning labor but still needs even moisture for uniform root size. Roots hold quality in the ground longer than older open-pollinated types, which makes Kestrel a dependable choice for succession plantings and for growers who bunch beets with their tops still attached. Harvest at 1.5-2.5 inches across for the sweetest, most tender roots.

common_name: Black Nebula Carrot (Deep Purple Skin and Flesh)

planting.note: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil once it can be worked; deep purple color is most intense on roots grown in cool spring or fall conditions.

directions: Black Nebula is a specialty carrot bred for pigment that runs all the way through the root rather than surrounding an orange core, giving nearly black-purple skin and a deep purple interior with only a faint lighter center. Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and keep the row consistently moist until germination, which is slower and less even than with standard orange carrots. The intense anthocyanin coloring holds up well in raw preparations, quick pickles, and shaved salads, though like other purple carrots it fades toward gray-brown if simmered without an acid. Thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart for well-formed roots and harvest at 70-80 days for full flavor and color development.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as the soil is workable in spring, in deep, loose, stone-free ground; parsnip seed viability drops quickly, so use current-year seed.

directions: Andover is a British-bred parsnip widely recognized for combining strong field resistance to canker with the smooth, well-shaped, medium-length roots gardeners expect from older heirlooms. It has become a standard recommendation in cool, damp growing regions where canker-prone varieties like Hollow Crown often develop the disfiguring rust-brown shoulder rot that ruins a crop. Sow shallowly and keep the seedbed evenly moist through the slow, uneven germination typical of parsnip, marking rows carefully since seedlings emerge slowly and are easy to lose to weeding. As with all parsnips, flavor sweetens dramatically after the roots experience several weeks of near-freezing temperatures, so delay harvest until after hard frost for the best eating quality.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed once soil can be worked in spring, into deep, loose, well-prepared ground free of stones and clods for straight, unforked roots.

directions: White Gem is an English garden parsnip selected for very pale, smooth skin, a bluntly wedge-shaped root, and good field tolerance to canker, making it a reliable choice where older heirloom types tend to scar and rot at the shoulder. Keep the bed consistently moist through slow, patchy germination and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding, which encourages forked roots. Its clean, uniform appearance and sweet, fine-grained flesh have made it a popular choice for both kitchen use and vegetable show competitions in the UK. Leave roots in the ground until after several hard frosts, since the cold converts starches to sugar and produces the variety's characteristic sweetness.
